summary:
Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns NASA Earth Information Center-style maps into sound in real time. A play head sweeps the map from west to east. At each longitude, ten latitude bands become notes on a pentatonic scale: pitch follows latitude, loudness follows data value, and stereo pan follows longitude. Each layer has its own timbre. Rising CO₂ and warming add detuning, while sharp changes between neighbouring latitudes speed up a pulse. Users can explore ocean heat, sea ice, vegetation, CO₂ and sea level, scrub through 1985–2025 or play it as a time-lapse, and load a real EIC frame, where color sets the key and mode.

The project answers the challenge by making EIC visualizations available through hearing as well as sight. It is fully keyboard-controllable, gives a text description of every image, buzzes on touch devices, and can record a one-sweep audio clip.

This matters because Earth science should not depend on vision. Sound makes change over time audible and emotional, for blind and low-vision users and for the wider public. The built-in layers are illustrative stand-ins; real NASA frames load through the upload button.
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Jukebox is an interactive web page that turns an Earth science map into live sound. A play head sweeps the map from west to east. At each longitude, the map is sampled at ten latitude bands, and each band drives one synthesizer voice.

Pitch follows latitude, with high notes in the north and low notes in the south, on a pentatonic scale so it stays musical.

Loudness follows the data value.

Stereo pan follows longitude, so you hear where you are on the globe.

Brightness and rhythm: the column average opens a filter, and sharp changes between neighbouring latitudes speed up a pulse.

Layers: ocean heat, sea ice, vegetation, CO₂ and sea level each have their own timbre. Rising CO₂ adds detuning.

Time: a year slider and time-lapse mode let you hear 1985 to 2025.

Real EIC frames: a loaded image is sonified from its pixels. Brightness sets loudness, and each column's dominant hue sets the key and mode (greens, blues and purples major; reds and oranges minor).

Benefits

  • Blind and low-vision users can explore Earth data that is otherwise only visual.
  • Sighted users get a second way to notice patterns and feel change over time.
  • It needs no install or account, runs on a phone or laptop, and keeps loaded images in the browser.

Intended impact

The aim is to make NASA's Earth Information Center content reachable by more people and to make climate change something you can hear: tension rising with warming and CO₂, and ice voices falling silent as ice retreats. It could also work as a teaching tool in classrooms.

Tools

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page
  • Web Audio API for the synthesis, filter, echo and panning
  • Canvas 2D for map rendering and reading image pixels
  • Media Recorder for recording a sweep, plus the Vibration API for touch feedback
  • No special hardware
  • Built with AI assistance from Claude. Say so in your submission if the rules ask for it.

Creativity

The "jukebox" is a scan of the map, so you listen along a path through the planet instead of hearing one static sound. The musical rules keep it pleasant, while urgency comes from the data itself. Color becoming harmony lets any EIC image work as a "song."

Factors considered

  • Accessibility: keyboard control, text descriptions and live captions of the sound.
  • Musicality versus accuracy: raw pixel mapping is noisy, so a scale and soft echo keep it listenable.
  • Honesty about data: the built-in layers are illustrative, procedurally generated stand-ins, not NASA measurements. Real frames load through upload, and brightness is only a proxy for value.
  • Limits: I haven't tested the app with blind or low-vision users or run it myself. Do both before you submit and list them as next steps.
